targetText:
The new value added by the annual newly added labour ; and thus also that
portion of the annual product in which this value is represented and which may
be drawn out of the total output and separated from it ; is thus split into
three parts, which assume three different forms of revenue, into forms which
express one portion of this value as belonging or falling to the share of the
owner of labour-power, another portion to the owner of capital, and a third
portion to the owner of landed property. These, then, are relations, or forms of
distribution, for they express the relations under which the newly produced
total value is distributed among the owners of the various production factors.
explanation: New value splits into three revenue streams: wages (to workers), profit (to capitalists), and rent (to landowners). These are not independent sources of wealth but divisions of a single surplus created by labor.

targetText:
From the common viewpoint these distribution relations appear as natural
relations, as relations arising directly from the nature of all social
production, from the laws of human production in general. It cannot, indeed, be
denied that pre-capitalist societies disclose other modes of distribution, but
the latter are interpreted as undeveloped, unperfected and disguised, not
reduced to their purest expression and their highest form and differently shaded
modes of the natural distribution relations.
explanation: Mainstream economics presents wages, profits, and rent as natural, eternal features of any economy. Marx argues they are historically specific to capitalism and reflect particular class power relations, not universal laws of nature.
